p: The Greeks called it Mesopotamia, the land between the rivers, and the name has stuck, as Greek names have a way of doing. The rivers are the Tigris and the Euphrates, which rise in the mountains of Armenia and flow south-east through what is now the Ottoman province of Baghdad, and, in the century to come, the kingdom and then republic of Iraq, until they reach the Persian Gulf. It is a flat land, hot and dry, where the rain is too scanty to grow crops but the soil, laid down by the floods of the rivers, is very rich if water can be brought to it. That condition, rich soil and no rain, is the key to everything that happened there.

To farm in southern Mesopotamia, people had to dig canals to carry the river water to their fields, and they had to maintain those canals, and to agree upon who should have the water and when. This required organisation on a scale unknown to a village. By about five and a half thousand years ago, in the land the ancients called Sumer, the villages had grown into towns and the towns into cities, the first true cities in the world. The greatest of them was Uruk, which by about three thousand years before Christ may have held forty thousand people or more, within a wall nearly ten kilometres around, that is to say about six miles. Other cities followed: Ur, Eridu, Lagash, Kish, Nippur and many more.

What is a city? It is not merely a large village. A city is a place where most people do not grow their own food. In Uruk there were priests and scribes, potters and weavers, smiths and brewers, merchants and soldiers, all of them fed by the surplus of the surrounding fields, which was gathered into the store-houses of the temple and redistributed according to rule. The temple was at the centre, both of the city and of its economy. Upon a great platform of mud brick, rising in stages toward the sky, stood the house of the city's god. Later, these stepped towers were called ziggurats, and it is very probable that the memory of one of them, at Babylon, lies behind the story in the Book of Genesis of the Tower of Babel.

At first, it seems, the cities were governed by their temples, and the chief priest was the chief man. In time, perhaps because the cities fought one another over water and land, war-leaders rose to power, and became kings, and made their office hereditary. The Sumerians recorded a list of kings, running back to times before a great flood, when kings were said to reign for tens of thousands of years apiece. The later entries are more modest and more believable. Every Sumerian city believed that it belonged to its god, and that the king was the god's steward; when one city conquered another, it was the god of the victor who had triumphed. This is a pattern we shall see again and again: the joining of earthly power to heavenly sanction, which has been useful to so many rulers and so dangerous to so many subjects.

Around two thousand three hundred years before Christ, a man named Sargon, who according to a later legend had been set adrift as a baby in a basket of reeds upon the river, rose to rule the city of Akkad, and conquered all the cities of Sumer and much besides. He is commonly called the first emperor in history. His dynasty did not last two centuries. After him came others: the kings of Ur, Hammurabi of Babylon, the Assyrians with their terrible armies, the later Babylonians under Nebuchadnezzar, who carried the Jews into captivity, and at last the Persians, who took Babylon in the year five hundred and thirty-nine before Christ. Mesopotamia was the stage on which empires first learned their trade.
## The gifts of the two rivers

Consider what came out of this land. Writing, which I shall treat separately, was invented here. So, very probably, was the wheel, or one of its first forms. So was the earliest written law. The Babylonians developed a system of counting based upon the number sixty, which you employ every time you look at a clock, for that is why there are sixty minutes in the hour and sixty seconds in the minute, and why a circle is divided into three hundred and sixty degrees. They observed the stars with great patience and kept records of the motions of the planets over centuries, records which the Greek astronomers inherited. They composed the oldest great poem we possess, the Epic of Gilgamesh, the story of a king of Uruk who seeks immortality and fails. Its tablets were found in the ruins of Nineveh by the English excavators of my own youth, and only three years ago, in eighteen seventy-two, a young man of the British Museum named George Smith, reading them, found among them the story of a great flood, with a man who builds a boat and sends out birds to find dry land, so like the story of Noah that he is said to have leapt up and begun undressing himself in his excitement. I was present at the lecture in which he announced it, and I can assure you that he kept his clothes on in public.

The fields that fed the first cities did not last for ever. Water carried over the land for many centuries left behind salt as it evaporated, and the soil of southern Mesopotamia slowly became poisoned. The Sumerians changed from wheat to barley, which tolerates salt better, and at last much of the land was abandoned. The great cities sank into mounds of mud brick, called tells, which rise from the plain to this day. Civilisation, it seems, can exhaust its own foundations. That is a lesson the men of the future, so the Encyclopaedia suggests, are learning again on a larger scale.
